title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: In October 1962 the United States found Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba. After a U-2 flight on 14 October, President Kennedy announced a naval quarantine on 22 October. On 28 October Khrushchev publicly agreed to remove the missiles. The 13-day standoff was the closest the superpowers came to nuclear war and led to the White House-Kremlin hotline.

uncertainty.note: Start is the U-2 photographs of 14 October; the crisis is widely called 13 days (History.com) counted from the White House briefing of 16 October to 28 October. The US quarantine ended 20 November 1962.

as_recorded.value: Oct. 14: A U-2 flight photographs ... missile sites under construction in Cuba; Oct. 28: Khrushchev publicly announces ... dismantled and removed
a tense, 13-day political and military standoff; Kennedy broadcast October 22, 1962

where.modern_name: Cuba and the surrounding Caribbean (pin at Havana)
where.historical_name: Republic of Cuba under Fidel Castro; crisis managed from Washington and Moscow

importance.justification: Closest nuclear confrontation of the Cold War; led to the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty.

related.because: Both Castro and Khrushchev saw the missiles as deterrence against further US aggression after the Bay of Pigs (History.com).

sources.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962
sources.publisher: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State

reviewer_note: Pin is Havana as a stand-in; decisions were taken in Washington and Moscow, and the quarantine ran across the Atlantic approaches. Start date uses the 14 October photographs; History.com counts 13 days. Jupiter missile removal from Turkey (April 1963) is a secret-deal element not stated as a public bargain.

beats.caption: A US U-2 flight photographed Soviet ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba.
Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba and demanded that the missiles be removed.
Khrushchev announced the Soviet missiles would be dismantled and removed, ending the standoff.
